summary: Provides a collection of additional matching rules for LDAP. They are simple adaptations of matching rules defined for the X.500 Directory, and most are already in wide use. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: When you search a directory, matching rules decide what counts as the same. This adds some more ways of comparing, borrowed from an older, bigger directory system.

questions: which rfc replaced rfc 2798 matching rule descriptions
subtitle: Twelve more ways for an LDAP directory to decide that two values match, borrowed from X.500.

tldr.problem: LDAP directories need rules that say when a search value matches a stored value, and several rules already used with X.500 directories were not yet written down for LDAP.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adapts twelve X.500 matching rules for LDAP, giving each one a plain description, an object identifier (OID) and the attribute syntax it applies to.
tldr.outcome: Most of the rules were already in wide use, for example with the inetOrgPerson and Policy Core schemas. The text replaces the matching rule descriptions in RFC 2798, and RFC 4517 later updated this RFC.

today: RFC 3698 is a Proposed Standard and is listed as updated by RFC 4517. It updates RFC 2798, taking over that RFC's matching rule descriptions.

sections.title: Background and Intended Use
sections.content:
RFC 3698 adapts additional matching rules from the X.500 Directory (described in X.520) for use with the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP). Most of them were already widely used on the Internet, for instance by the inetOrgPerson and Policy Core Information Model LDAP schemas, and the RFC says they apply to many other applications too.

The document also tidies up an earlier one. It supersedes the informational matching rule descriptions that were in RFC 2798: section 2 of this RFC replaces section 9.3.3 of that one. That is why the metadata lists RFC 3698 as updating RFC 2798.
sections.eli5: A directory already knew some ways to compare names. This paper writes down twelve more that people were already using, so everyone describes them the same way.

sections.title: How Each Rule Is Defined
sections.content:
A matching rule tells a directory server how to compare an asserted value (what a search asks for) with an attribute value (what is stored). Every rule here gets the same treatment: a short prose definition, a note of its source (X.520), and a schema definition written in the LDAP description format from RFC 2252.

A definition has the form ( 2.5.13.13 NAME 'booleanMatch' SYNTAX 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.115.121.1.7 ). It carries the rule's OID, its name, and the OID of the syntax it expects for the stored value. The RFC says the line wrapping is only for readability.

The syntaxes used are all described in RFC 2252: BOOLEAN, DirectoryString, SubstringsAssertion, INTEGER, NumericString and OCTET STRING.
sections.eli5: Each rule comes with a name tag, a number and a note saying what kind of thing it compares, like a label on a drawer in a filing cabinet.

sections.title: Equality and Substring Rules
sections.content:
Several rules decide whether a stored value equals, or contains, what was asked for.

  • booleanMatch returns TRUE if and only if both values are TRUE or both are FALSE.
  • caseExactMatch is identical to caseIgnoreMatch except that case is not ignored.
  • caseExactSubstringsMatch is identical to caseIgnoreSubstringsMatch except that case is not ignored.
  • caseIgnoreListSubstringsMatch works on a stored value that is a sequence of DirectoryStrings. It matches the concatenation of those strings, but no initial, any or final part of the asserted value may span more than one of the stored strings.
  • directoryStringFirstComponentMatch looks only at the first component of a stored SEQUENCE, which must be a DirectoryString, and compares it using caseIgnoreMatch.
sections.eli5: Some rules are like asking whether two words are exactly the same, with capital letters counting. Others check whether a small piece of text appears inside a bigger one.

sections.title: Ordering Rules
sections.content:
Ordering rules compare which value comes first, which supports greater-than or less-than style searches.

  • caseExactOrderingMatch is identical to caseIgnoreOrderingMatch except that letters are not folded.
  • integerOrderingMatch returns True if the attribute value is less than the asserted value.
  • numericStringOrderingMatch is identical to caseIgnoreOrderingMatch except that all space characters are skipped during comparison.
  • octetStringOrderingMatch compares octets from first to last and bits from most to least significant. The first different bit decides, a zero bit precedes a one bit, and if the strings are otherwise identical the shorter one comes first.
sections.eli5: Ordering rules are like lining kids up by height or words up like in a dictionary, so you can tell who goes before whom.

sections.title: Keyword, Word and Prefix Rules
sections.content:
Three rules match parts of a stored string rather than the whole of it.

  • keywordMatch returns TRUE if and only if the asserted value matches any keyword in the attribute value. How keywords are identified, and how exact the match is, are implementation specific.
  • wordMatch returns TRUE if and only if the asserted word matches any word in the attribute value, using caseIgnoreMatch for each word. What counts as a word is implementation specific.
  • storedPrefixMatch returns TRUE if and only if the stored value is an initial substring of the asserted value, ignoring case. Note the direction: the stored value is the prefix.

The RFC gives one example use for storedPrefixMatch: comparing stored telephone area codes with a purported value that is a full telephone number.
sections.eli5: These rules look for a single word inside a sentence, or check that a short stored label like an area code is the start of a longer phone number.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security section is brief. It says that the general LDAP security considerations from RFC 3377 apply to use of this schema, and that additional considerations are noted in the rule descriptions where appropriate. It adds no new security mechanism of its own.
sections.eli5: The safety rules for the directory are the ones that already exist. This paper does not add new ones.

sections.title: IANA Registry Updates
sections.content:
IANA updated the LDAP descriptors registry (from RFC 3383) to add all twelve names as Type M, meaning matching rule, each with its OID. The contact and change controller are given as Kurt Zeilenga and the IESG.

The RFC makes no new OID assignments. It only associates LDAP matching rule descriptions with existing X.500 matching rules.
sections.eli5: The official list of names got twelve new entries. The numbers were already handed out earlier, so nothing new was invented.

items.label: caseExactOrderingMatch
items.desc: Ordering of DirectoryStrings, letters not folded.

items.label: caseIgnoreListSubstringsMatch
items.desc: Substring match across a sequence of strings, without spanning.

items.label: directoryStringFirstComponentMatch
items.desc: Equality on the first component of a SEQUENCE.

items.label: keywordMatch
items.desc: Matches any keyword in the stored value.

items.label: storedPrefixMatch
items.desc: Stored value is a prefix of the asserted value.

items.label: wordMatch
items.desc: Matches any word in the stored value.
